endorsements.title: Balancing Innovation and Control: The European Union AI Act in an Era of Global Uncertainty
endorsements.quote: Procurement policies can also serve as a powerful lever: health care systems can favor vendors that demonstrate ethical compliance, much like environmental or labor standards in other sectors [ 31 ].

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether defined procurement requirements and competitive vendor selection reduce the rate of unsupported, poorly integrated, or unstable AI products, and no study documents how often ad hoc selection produces those outcomes. Five sources endorse the practice, but two of the supplied quotations address other topics, so the recommendation rests on a narrower base of expert opinion than the count implies.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests the practice or documents the hazard, so certainty under GRADE conventions is no direct evidence. The endorsements comprise one framework, three guidance documents, and one commentary. The quotations from the CHAI playbooks and from the principles for augmented intelligence concern privacy notices and digital literacy rather than vendor selection.

The multi-society radiology statement asks buyers to weigh vendor reliability, staying power under limited reimbursement, and consolidation risk. Those criteria describe what a procurement checklist might contain. No supplied study reports the staff time, cost, or cycle length of a structured competitive process, or compares vendor failure rates with and without one.

The EU AI Act commentary describes procurement as a way for health systems to favor vendors that show ethical compliance, by analogy to environmental and labor standards. This is an argument by analogy. No supplied study shows that procurement terms change vendor disclosure or compliance behavior in health care.

The adoption report on AI in delivery systems states that common data pipelines and interoperable enterprise systems are needed as AI tools multiply. This supports including integration criteria in selection. No supplied study measures whether integration requirements written into procurement improve post-deployment fit with clinical workflows.

commentary.research_gap: Health systems lack studies that compare structured, competitive AI procurement with ad hoc selection on outcomes such as integration failures, vendor exit or product discontinuation, support responsiveness, clinician adoption, and total cost. Descriptive studies are also missing that establish how often ad hoc selection leads to unstable or unsupported products. Such studies would show whether the hazard is common enough to justify the process burden.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence exists on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net systems may have fewer procurement staff and less bargaining power with vendors. Whether a formal competitive process is feasible for them, or whether selection criteria should cover language access and readability of patient-facing outputs, remains untested.
